claims.text: FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a strongly size-dependent thermal response.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a lower effective melting temperature than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo surface-mediated phase transitions earlier than larger particles.
Near-equiatomic FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles can be synthesized with controlled size distributions.
Molecular dynamics simulations can be used to investigate the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
A tailored FeCuCrCoNi interatomic potential can model heating and cooling cycles.
A simulated temperature interval from room temperature to approximately 973 K is suitable for studying nanoparticle thermal evolution.
The proposed simulations span particle sizes from below 10 nm to tens of nanometers.
Heating FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles enhances surface atomic diffusion and may cause surface elemental segregation.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio magnifies the influence of surface energy on nanoparticle thermal behavior.
Increased surface atomic mobility can promote surface phase separation and melting.
Greater surface atomic mobility lowers the onset temperatures for melting and phase separation in smaller particles.
Atomistic simulations can capture temperature-driven atomic diffusion, surface segregation, and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Under identical thermal loading, the smallest FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will melt or substantially restructure at lower temperatures than larger particles.
Surface effects are less dominant in larger nanoparticles and bulk material.
Simulation results may be sensitive to the accuracy of the interatomic potential.
Simulations that omit oxidation and support interactions may not capture corresponding experimental effects.
In situ heating electron microscopy can be combined with molecular dynamics to compare atomic-scale thermal transformations.
Failure to observe a lower transition onset temperature in smaller particles, or failure of simulations to reproduce that trend, would falsify the stated hypothesis.
